sources.title: RBI: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
sources.supports: title and update date read on rbi.org.in 2026-10-05; the PDF on rbidocs.rbi.org.in sits behind a CAPTCHA, so its recovery-agent rules (8:00 a.m.-7:00 p.m. calling window, no inappropriate social-media messages) are from a web-search summary only

sources.title: RBI: Master Circular - Fair Practices Code (NBFCs), 1 Jul 2015
sources.supports: vernacular-language communications, no harassment at odd hours (historic text, consolidated into the 2025 Directions)

sources.title: RBI: Recovery Agents engaged by banks, 24 Apr 2008
sources.supports: agent must carry the bank's notice, authorisation letter and identity card; training on hours of calling and privacy

sources.title: RBI/2022-23/108: Responsibilities of regulated entities employing recovery agents (Aug 2022)
sources.supports: origin of the 8 a.m.-7 p.m. calling restriction across commercial banks, co-operative banks, NBFCs, ARCs and AIFIs (behind CAPTCHA; known from search summary)

cards.summary: Status as read 2026-10-05: RBI consolidated its instructions into entity-wise Directions in 2025, and the NBFC Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 are 'Updated as on July 1, 2026' (rbi.org.in). The Directions' own PDF sat behind a CAPTCHA that was not bypassed, so rules 3 and 4 below come from older RBI texts and a web-search summary: read the current Direction for the entity type (bank, NBFC, co-operative bank) before quoting any of this.
use_for: Writing EMI reminders, overdue-loan SMS, WhatsApp and email copy for a bank or NBFC
Writing recovery-agent call scripts and IVR messages
Writing loan-offer copy that must also respect the lender's fair-practices duties
avoid: Threats, shaming or any line meant to humiliate publicly ('your family and employer will be told'). RBI bars acts intended to humiliate publicly or intrude on the privacy of family members and friends.
A collection message that does not say who is writing. Name the lender and, if one is acting, the recovery agency.
A message in English only for a borrower who reads Hindi or another language. Communicate in the vernacular language or a language the borrower understands.
Scripting or scheduling calls before 8:00 a.m. or after 7:00 p.m. for an overdue loan.
Posting about a borrower on social media or sending inappropriate messages, whatever the tone.
cards.jurisdiction: India (RBI-regulated banks and NBFCs; read the Direction for your entity type)

rules.rule: 'All communications to the borrower shall be in the vernacular language or a language as understood by the borrower' (RBI Master Circular, Fair Practices Code for NBFCs, 1 Jul 2015, para 2A(i)(a); historic text, since consolidated into the 2025 Directions).

Lenders 'should not resort to undue harassment viz; persistently bothering the borrowers at odd hours, use muscle power for recovery of loans' (same 2015 Master Circular, recovery paragraph; historic text).

Secondary (web-search summary of RBI/2022-23/108 and the 2025 Directions; the PDFs were behind a CAPTCHA and not read): no intimidation or harassment of any kind, verbal or physical; no acts 'intended to humiliate publicly' or that intrude on the privacy of family members and friends; no inappropriate messages on mobile or social media; no threatening or anonymous calls; no persistent calls before 8:00 a.m. or after 7:00 p.m. for overdue loans.

The borrower must be told which recovery agency is acting, and the agent carries 'the notice and the authorization letter from the bank along with the identity card' (RBI circular, 24 Apr 2008); collection messages should therefore name the lender and the agency.

checks: Is the message in a language the borrower understands, in the vernacular where needed?
Does it name the lender and, if an agency is acting, the recovery agency?
Is it free of threats, abuse, public humiliation and any reference to the borrower's family or friends?
Is it free of anything meant for social media or an inappropriate mobile message about the borrower?
Does the script avoid calls before 8:00 a.m. or after 7:00 p.m.?
Has the current Direction for the entity type (bank, NBFC, co-operative bank) been read before any rule is quoted?

cards.name: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016: advertising a real-estate project (registration number, Authority website, carpet area, veracity) and state RERA orders

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: Section 11 in the RERA Act, 2016
sources.supports: s.11(2) text: ad must mention Authority website and registration number (secondary; India Code PDF unreachable 2026-10-05)

sources.title: Lawsisto: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (full text)
sources.supports: s.2(b) advertisement, s.2(k) carpet area, s.3(1) no advertising before registration, s.12 compensation for false statements (secondary reproduction, read via fetch summary)

sources.title: MahaRERA: Suo Motu Advertisement Case No. 43 of 2024
sources.supports: quotes MahaRERA Order No. 46/2023 (29.05.2023) and 46A/2023 (25.07.2023): QR code beside registration number and website on every ad after 01.08.2023

sources.title: MahaRERA: Orders and Circulars
sources.supports: index of state orders incl. Order No. 46C/2025 on QR code and font size of the registration number (search listing; not read)

cards.summary: The Act is in force (central text read on 2026-10-05 only through secondary reproductions because India Code was unreachable: medium confidence); each state has its own RERA rules and authority orders. A builder's ad, brochure, hoarding or social post may run only for a RERA-registered project, must show the registration number and the Authority's website prominently (Maharashtra also requires a QR code), and every claim in it is something the promoter must compensate for if false.
use_for: Writing property ads, brochures, hoardings, reels, WhatsApp forwards and listing pages for an Indian developer
Writing area, amenity and possession-date copy that must match the registered project
Pre-launch teaser copy: deciding whether it can run before registration
avoid: A 'pre-launch', 'EOI' or 'bookings open soon' teaser before the project is registered. Section 3(1) bars advertising, marketing or inviting purchase of a plot, apartment or building in a project that needs registration without registering it.
An ad with no registration number or no Authority website address. Put both prominently; in Maharashtra add the QR code beside them.
Quoting a flat's size as super built-up area. State the carpet area as the Act defines it.
Promising amenities, possession dates or approvals that the registered project does not show. A buyer who suffers loss from an incorrect or false statement in the ad is compensated by the promoter.
Copying a Maharashtra ad format into another state. Check the project's own state RERA orders.
cards.jurisdiction: India (central RERA Act, 2016; state RERA rules and authority orders; Maharashtra example)

rules.rule: 'Advertisement' means 'any document described or issued as advertisement through any medium and includes any notice, circular or other documents or publicity in any form' (s.2(b)): brochures, hoardings, WhatsApp forwards, reels and listing pages all fall within it (the last part is the harvest item's reading) (Lawsisto, secondary).

'No promoter shall advertise, market, book, sell or offer for sale, or invite persons to purchase in any manner' a plot, apartment or building in a project that needs registration without registering it (s.3(1)): no 'pre-launch' or 'EOI' teasers before registration (Lawsisto, secondary).

'The advertisement or prospectus ... shall mention prominently the website address of the Authority ... and include the registration number obtained from the Authority' (s.11(2)) (Indian Kanoon, secondary).

Carpet area is 'the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding ... external walls, ... services shafts, exclusive balcony or verandah area and exclusive open terrace area' (s.2(k)); quote sizes as carpet area, not an inflated super built-up figure (Lawsisto, secondary).
A buyer who pays on the basis of the advertisement and suffers loss 'by reason of any incorrect, false statement included therein' must be compensated by the promoter (s.12) (Lawsisto, secondary).

Maharashtra: 'The Promoter shall prominently display QR Code on each and every project promotion/advertisement published after 01.08.2023' beside the MahaRERA registration number and website address (MahaRERA Order No. 46/2023 of 29.05.2023 and 46A/2023 of 25.07.2023, as quoted in Suo Motu Advertisement Case No. 43 of 2024).

MahaRERA has since issued Order No. 46C/2025 on the QR code and the font size of the registration number; it appears in MahaRERA's order index (search listing) and was not read, so its content is unconfirmed.

cards.penalty: Compensation to a buyer who paid on the basis of the advertisement and lost money from an incorrect or false statement in it (s.12, secondary text). Other penalties are not recorded in this card.
checks: Is the project registered with the state RERA before any advertisement, teaser, EOI or booking invitation goes out?
Does the piece show the RERA registration number and the Authority's website address prominently?
For a Maharashtra project, is there a QR code beside the registration number and website on every promotion published after 01.08.2023, and has Order 46C/2025 on QR code and font size been checked?
Are sizes quoted as carpet area as the Act defines it, not an inflated super built-up figure?
Do amenities, possession dates, approvals and layouts match the registered project?
Do WhatsApp forwards, reels and listing pages carry the same registration details as the brochure?
Has the project's own state RERA orders page been checked for rules beyond the central Act?

cards.name: Representation of the People Act, 1951 section 123: corrupt practices (religion / caste appeals, promoting enmity, false statements about candidates)

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: Section 123 in The Representation of the People Act, 1951
sources.supports: current text of s.123 clauses (1)-(8): bribery, undue influence, appeals on religion etc., enmity, sati, false statements (secondary reproduction; India Code refused fetch 2026-10-05)

cards.summary: In force (the statute text of s.123 was read on Indian Kanoon 2026-10-05; India Code refused the fetch, so medium confidence). Section 123 applies to the candidate, the agent or 'any other person with the consent of a candidate or his election agent', which covers an agency or writer producing campaign copy. Election slogans, speeches, ads and posts may not appeal for votes on religion, race, caste, community or language, use religious or national symbols, stoke enmity between groups, or publish false statements of fact about a rival's character.
use_for: Writing election slogans, speeches, manifestos, ads and social posts for a candidate or party
Checking satire and attack content about rivals before release
Reviewing giveaway or contest copy that touches voting
avoid: 'Vote for your own community' or any appeal on religion, race, caste, community or language. Make the case on record, policy and promises.
Using the national flag, the national emblem or a religious symbol to win votes. (The party symbol allotted under the Act is not a religious or national symbol for this purpose.)
A stated fact about a rival's personal character or conduct that is false or not checked. Use documented facts, or clearly framed opinion and satire.
A threat of divine displeasure or spiritual censure. A declaration of public policy or a promise of public action is fine.
Giveaway, gift or contest copy tied to voting. Bribery covers any gratification to an elector, including entertainment.
cards.jurisdiction: India (Representation of the People Act, 1951)

rules.rule: No appeal 'to vote or refrain from voting for any person on the ground of his religion, race, caste, community or language', and no use of or appeal to religious symbols or 'national symbols, such as the national flag or the national emblem' to further a candidate's prospects; the party symbol allotted under the Act is not a religious or national symbol for this purpose (s.123(3)).
No 'promotion of, or attempt to promote, feelings of enmity or hatred between different classes ... on grounds of religion, race, caste, community, or language' (s.123(3A)).

No publication 'of any statement of fact which is false', believed false or not believed true, about 'the personal character or conduct of any candidate' or about anyone's candidature or withdrawal, reasonably calculated to hurt their prospects (s.123(4)). Satire and opinion are safer than invented facts (the harvest item's reading).
Threatening voters with 'divine displeasure or spiritual censure' is undue influence, but 'a declaration of public policy, or a promise of public action' is not (s.123(2)).
Bribery covers any gratification to an elector, including entertainment (s.123(1)): giveaway or contest copy tied to voting is out (the last part is the harvest item's reading).

checks: Does any slogan, speech line, ad or post avoid asking for votes on religion, race, caste, community or language?
Is the piece free of religious symbols and of the national flag or emblem used to further the candidate?
Is it free of any line that promotes enmity or hatred between classes of citizens on those grounds?
Is every statement of fact about a rival's personal character or conduct true and documented, or clearly opinion or satire?
Is there no threat of divine displeasure or spiritual censure (a policy promise is fine)?
Is there no gift, giveaway or contest copy tied to voting?
Has the piece also been checked against the Model Code of Conduct and the printer-and-publisher imprint rule (comp:eci_mcc, comp:rpa_s127a_election_print)?

cards.name: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015: material-event disclosure (Reg 30), annual report MD&A and BRSR

sources.title: SEBI: LODR Regulations, 2015 [Last amended on July 14, 2026]
sources.supports: official consolidated text page; PDF https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/jul-2026/1784630770711.pdf read 2026-10-05

sources.title: SEBI: LODR Regulations, 2015 consolidated text (PDF, amended up to July 14, 2026)
sources.supports: text of Reg 4, Reg 30(6), 30(8), 30(11), Reg 34(2)(f) and Schedule V Part B, read 2026-10-05

sources.title: SEBI: FAQs for LODR Regulations (Apr 2025)
sources.supports: SEBI's own FAQ on the regulations (not read in full)

cards.summary: In force; SEBI's consolidated text is 'Last amended on July 14, 2026' (PDF read 2026-10-05). For a listed company, material events go to the stock exchanges first, within fixed hours, and everything the company puts out (press release, shareholder letter, annual report) must be accurate, not misleading and in simple language.
use_for: Writing press releases, shareholder letters, social posts and CEO letters for a listed company
Writing the MD&A and BRSR parts of an annual report
Sequencing a material announcement: exchange filing first, then everything else
avoid: Publishing a press release, post or shareholder letter about a material event before the stock-exchange filing. Reg 30 puts the exchange first.
Promotional or vague language in an exchange or investor disclosure. Reg 4 asks for information that is adequate, accurate, explicit, timely and in simple language.
Ignoring a media rumour that moves the share price. A top-listed entity must confirm, deny or clarify within 24 hours of a material price movement.
An MD&A that is a glossy story with no risks, outlook or internal-controls discussion. Cover each head Schedule V Part B lists.
cards.jurisdiction: India (SEBI; listed entities)

rules.rule: Reg 4: the listed entity 'shall refrain from misrepresentation and ensure that the information provided to recognised stock exchange(s) and investors is not misleading', and disseminations must be 'adequate, accurate, explicit, timely and presented in a simple language'.

Reg 30(6): material events or information go to the stock exchange(s) first, within 30 minutes of the board meeting closing (3 hours if it closes after market hours), 12 hours if the event emanates from within the company, 24 hours if from outside; a late disclosure must carry an explanation for the delay. A press release, social post or shareholder letter about a material event must not go out before the exchange filing (the last part is the harvest item's reading).
Reg 30(8): the same events are placed on the company's website.

Reg 30(11): top 100, then top 250, listed entities must confirm, deny or clarify a specific mainstream-media rumour within 24 hours of a material price movement; if confirming, they give the current stage (the item gives the cut-offs without dates).

Schedule V Part B: the annual report includes a Management Discussion and Analysis covering industry structure, opportunities and threats, segment performance, outlook, risks and concerns, internal controls, financial versus operational performance and human-resource developments.
Reg 34(2)(f): for the top 1,000 listed entities by market capitalisation, the annual report includes a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR).

checks: Has the stock-exchange filing gone out before any press release, social post or shareholder letter about the material event is published?
Is every figure and claim accurate, explicit and not misleading, in simple language?
If a disclosure is late, does it carry the reason for the delay?
Is the same event on the company website?
For a top-listed entity facing a media rumour, is there a confirm, deny or clarify response within 24 hours of a material price movement, giving the current stage if confirmed?

Does the MD&A cover every head: industry structure, opportunities and threats, segment performance, outlook, risks and concerns, internal controls, financial versus operational performance, HR developments?
If the company is in the top 1,000 by market capitalisation, is a BRSR included?
Have the filing deadlines been checked against Reg 30(6) before any timing is promised in copy?

cards.name: SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015: UPSI, fair-disclosure code and trading window

sources.title: SEBI: PIT Regulations, 2015 [Last amended on March 12, 2025]
sources.supports: official consolidated text page; PDF https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/aug-2026/1786963663321.pdf ('Amended upto March 12, 2025', includes amendments w.e.f. June 10, 2025) read 2026-10-05

sources.title: SEBI: Comprehensive FAQs on PIT Regulations (Apr 2025)
sources.supports: SEBI's own FAQ (not read in full)

cards.summary: In force; SEBI's consolidated text is 'Amended upto March 12, 2025' and includes amendments effective June 10, 2025 (PDF read 2026-10-05). Unpublished price-sensitive information about a listed company may not be leaked, teased or selectively shared in IR, PR or social copy; it must be released uniformly to everyone at once.
use_for: Writing investor-relations, PR and social copy for a listed company around results and corporate events
Handling drafts of results, press releases and CEO letters inside the quiet period
Briefing an agency or ghostwriter on what must not be hinted at before disclosure
avoid: A teaser, 'big news coming' post, interview line or analyst-deck slide that hints at results, a dividend, M&A, fund raising, a rating change or a large contract before the exchange disclosure.
Treating a leak as public. Information reported in the media that is unverified does not become 'generally available'.
Sharing a results draft widely with the agency, freelancers or the social team. Limit it to people who need it for legitimate purposes, duties or legal obligations.
Giving UPSI to an analyst in a call or meeting; records of analyst and IR meetings go on the official website.
cards.jurisdiction: India (SEBI; listed companies, insiders and connected persons)

rules.rule: UPSI is information 'not generally available which upon becoming generally available, is likely to materially affect the price', ordinarily including financial results, dividends, changes in capital structure, mergers and acquisitions, large contract wins or losses outside the normal course, changes in key managerial personnel, rating changes, fund raising, and fraud or defaults (Reg 2(1)(n)).

'No insider shall communicate, provide, or allow access to any unpublished price sensitive information' except for 'legitimate purposes, performance of duties or discharge of legal obligations' (Reg 3(1)).

'Generally available information' is information accessible on a non-discriminatory basis and 'shall not include unverified event or information reported in print or electronic media' (Reg 2(1)(e)): a news leak does not make it public.

Fair-disclosure principles (Schedule A): prompt public disclosure; 'Uniform and universal dissemination ... to avoid selective disclosure'; information shared with analysts must not be UPSI; transcripts or records of analyst and IR meetings go on the official website.

The trading window for designated persons is closed from the end of every quarter until 48 hours after results (Schedule B); results-season copy and insider quotes are drafted inside that quiet period, so drafts stay need-to-know (the last part is the harvest item's reading).

checks: Does the piece avoid hints about results, dividends, M&A, fund raising, rating changes, key-personnel changes, large contracts, fraud or defaults before the exchange disclosure, including teasers and 'big news coming' posts?
Has the draft been shared only with people who need it for legitimate purposes, duties or legal obligations?
Is no unverified media report treated as public information?
Is the same information being released to everyone at once, with any analyst or IR meeting record headed for the website?
If the piece is drafted in the trading-window quiet period, is it handled as need-to-know?
Does the piece avoid giving UPSI to an analyst or interviewer?

cards.name: Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP) 2024: what drug promotion and medical-detailing copy may claim

sources.supports: full code text: general points, claims and comparisons, promotional material, brand reminders (company-hosted copy of the government code; pharmaceuticals.gov.in not fetched)

cards.summary: UCPMP 2024 was issued by the Department of Pharmaceuticals and is dated 12 March 2024; the text was read 2026-10-05 in a copy hosted by a drug company (medium confidence; pharmaceuticals.gov.in was not fetched). A drug's marketing approval itself comes from CDSCO under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 (not read in this pass). Pharma promotion to doctors may start only after marketing approval, must be balanced and substantiable, may not call a drug 'safe' without qualification or 'new' after a year, and must carry the prescribing basics.
use_for: Writing medical-detailing leaflets, visual aids, journal ads and brand reminders for prescribers
Reviewing pharma copy for unqualified 'safe', 'new' and comparison claims
Writing prescriber-facing mailers
avoid: Promotion before the drug has marketing approval, or an indication outside the approval. Promotion must be consistent with the terms of the marketing approval.
'Safe' with no qualification, or 'no side effects'. Use the evidence: what was studied, in whom, and the adverse reactions.
'New' on a drug generally available or promoted in India for more than a year.
Naming a competitor's brand without its prior consent, or belittling another company or a doctor's opinion. Compare factually and fairly, with substantiation.
Using a prescriber-facing claim in public copy. Public-facing cure claims fall under the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act (comp:dmr_act_1954).
cards.jurisdiction: India (Department of Pharmaceuticals; drug promotion to healthcare professionals)
applies_to: medical detailing leaflets and brand reminders

rules.rule: Para 1.2: 'a drug must not be promoted prior to receipt of its marketing approval', and promotion 'must be consistent with the terms of its marketing approval': no off-label indications.
Para 1.3: information 'must be balanced, up-to-date, verifiable, must not mislead either directly or by implication' and 'must be capable of substantiation' on request.

Paras 2.2-2.3: the word 'safe' must not be used without qualification, and categorical 'no side effects' claims are out; the word 'new' must not be used for a drug generally available or promoted in India for more than a year.
Paras 2.4-2.7: comparisons must be factual, fair and substantiable; no competitor brand names without their prior consent; no disparaging other companies or doctors' opinions.

Para 3.2: promotional material for prescribers must include the authorisation holder's name and address, the generic names of the active ingredients adjacent to the brand name, dosage and method of use, adverse reactions, warnings, precautions and contraindications, and the date the particulars were last updated.

Paras 3.3, 3.6 and 3.9: paid journal pieces must not resemble editorial matter; no names or photographs of healthcare professionals; exposed mailings must not carry matter that reads as advertising to the lay public.

checks: Is the drug approved for marketing, and does every claim stay within the approved indication?
Is every statement balanced, up to date, verifiable and substantiable on request?
Is 'safe' always qualified, and are 'no side effects' claims absent?
Is 'new' used only for a drug available or promoted in India for a year or less?
Are comparisons factual and fair, with competitor brands named only with their prior consent and no disparagement?

Does prescriber-facing material show the authorisation holder's name and address, generic names beside the brand name, dosage and method of use, adverse reactions, warnings, precautions, contraindications and the last-updated date?

Does a paid journal piece look like an advertisement rather than editorial, with no names or photographs of healthcare professionals, and does an exposed mailing carry nothing that reads as advertising to the lay public?

cards.name: YouTube Spam Policy (malicious clickbait, misleading metadata and thumbnails, scams, engagement manipulation, mass-produced AI content)

sources.title: YouTube Help: Spam Policy (formerly 'Spam, deceptive practices, and scams policies')
sources.supports: full current policy: scope incl. titles, thumbnails, links, comments; examples for each violation type; enforcement (warning, strikes, termination, monetisation)

cards.summary: Current page read 2026-10-05. It is now titled 'Spam Policy' (formerly 'Spam, deceptive practices, and scams policies') and sits beside separate Impersonation, External links and Fake engagement policies. YouTube bans titles, thumbnails and descriptions that promise what the video does not deliver, scam and get-rich-quick pitches, engagement bait, comment spam, scraped re-uploads and mass-produced repetitive AI videos.
use_for: Writing YouTube titles, thumbnails text, descriptions and community posts that stay within the policy
Writing calls to action that ask for likes, comments and subscribes within the rules
Checking an AI-assisted or high-volume channel plan for mass-production risk
avoid: A title or thumbnail that promises a full match, a result or a reveal that the video does not contain. A curiosity title is fine only if the video pays it off.
Rewards for likes, views or subscribers, sub-for-sub schemes or high volumes of low-effort, repetitive polls. Asking viewers to like, comment or subscribe is fine.
Get-rich-quick investment pitches, fake job offers or fake customer-support numbers in the copy or description.
A video made solely to drive viewers off YouTube.
The same music, AI imagery and AI-read script across many videos with minimal changes, or re-uploads with no original commentary, educational value or unique editing.
cards.jurisdiction: YouTube (global platform policy)

rules.rule: The policy covers more than the video: 'This policy applies to all types of content on YouTube, including unlisted and private content, comments, links, posts and thumbnails'.

Malicious clickbait is 'Using maliciously misleading titles, thumbnails, descriptions, or imagery to trick users into clicking on a video that does not deliver what was promised' (example: a title offering a full sports match when the video is a clip). A curiosity title the video pays off is fine; one it does not pay off is not (the last part is the harvest item's reading).
'It's okay to ask viewers to like, comment, or subscribe', but not to offer rewards for likes, views or subscribers, run sub-for-sub schemes, or post 'high volumes of low-effort, repetitive polls'.
No scam copy: 'get rich quick' investment schemes, fake job offers, fake customer-support numbers; no videos 'created solely to drive users off of YouTube'.

'Automated or synthetic mass-production' is banned: using AI 'to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes' (example: the same music and AI imagery with an AI-read script across many videos); re-uploads need 'original commentary, educational value, or unique editing'.

cards.penalty: Removal; a warning, then strikes ('3 strikes within 90 days' can terminate the channel); suspended monetisation (YouTube Help, Spam Policy).
checks: Does the title, thumbnail and description deliver exactly what the video shows?
Is every promised item (full match, result, reveal) actually in the video?
Does the call to action ask for a like, comment or subscribe without a reward, a sub-for-sub offer or repetitive polls?
Is the copy free of get-rich-quick pitches, fake job offers and fake customer-support numbers?
Is the video made for viewers on YouTube, not solely to drive them off it?
If AI-assisted or repurposed, does each video differ materially from the others, and does any re-upload add original commentary, educational value or unique editing?
